unit.title: Ratios and valuation
unit.description: P/E, PEG, EV/EBITDA, ROE, dividends, DCF and CAPE with real numbers

texts: The P/E with growth
This share trades on a **P/E of 20**. But paying 20 years of earnings for a company that barely grows isn't the same as paying it for one that's flying.
Two companies on a P/E of 20. A grows 20 % a year; B, 5 %. Which is cheaper?
A, the one growing faster
B, the one growing slower
Both the same: they have the same P/E
A's PEG: 20 ÷ 20 = **1**. B's PEG: 20 ÷ 5 = **4**. With A you pay much less for each point of growth.
With the price at €20, find the growth that brings the PEG down to 1.
**PEG = P/E ÷ annual earnings growth.** Close to 1, reasonable; above 2, **expensive for its growth**. Panadería Global: 15.4 ÷ 8 = 1.9.
A PEG of 1! The price is in line with its growth.
You're paying a lot for very little growth.
Turn up the growth and watch the PEG
Two flats, same price
Nora
Two identical flats are for sale at €100,000 each.
The second one has an €80,000 mortgage that I'd take over.
But they cost the same, right?
Which one really costs more?
Both the same: €100,000
The second costs €100,000 plus the debt you inherit: **€180,000**.
The second: you're buying the flat and its debt
Exactly: €180,000 versus €100,000. It's the same with companies.
It depends on the area
Here they're identical. The difference is the debt.
That's **enterprise value (EV)**: market cap plus net debt.
You compare it with **EBITDA**. Panadería Global: (1,500 + 320) ÷ 200 = **9.1**.
Each company, its ratio
No ratio works for everything. Which would you look at first for each company?
PEG
EV/EBITDA
Price / book value
A bank
Its balance sheet is full of financial assets: P/B.
A tech company growing 25 % a year
What matters most is how fast it grows: PEG.
An industrial company with lots of debt
EV/EBITDA brings the debt into the sum; the P/E can't see it.
An insurer
Like a bank, it's valued mainly on its balance sheet.
A chain of shops growing 20 %
It's growing fast: compare its P/E with that growth.
A heavily indebted utility
With that much debt, market cap is misleading: look at EV.
A fast-growing software company
It's valued for its ideas, not its assets: P/B tells you little.
Place the seven companies.
Each ratio sheds light on one thing: **PEG**, growth; **EV/EBITDA**, debt; **P/B**, the balance sheet. Choose the ratio to suit the type of company.
Ask yourself: what matters most here, growth, debt or the balance sheet?
Choose the ratio for each company

steps.title: P/B: for banks and insurers
steps.body:
**P/B = price ÷ book value per share.** Panadería Global: 15 ÷ 4.5 = **3.3**.

It's used mainly for banks and insurers, whose balance sheets are full of financial assets. For a software company, which is valued for its ideas rather than its assets, it tells you very little.
steps.key: Choose the ratio to suit the type of company.
steps.tip: Try it: ask Lumi when a high P/E can be justified.

u17l3.title: ROE and ROIC: is it a good business?

texts: Two lemonade stands
Ana
Bruno
Ana and Bruno set up the same lemonade stand. Each needs €1,000. No taxes, to keep it simple.
I put in the €1,000 out of my own pocket. I make €200 a year.
I put in €200 and borrow €800. After paying €40 in interest, I make €160.
Who has the better business?
Bruno: he makes 80 % on his money
An **ROE** of 80 %, yes. But the stand is identical: it's the debt.
It's the same business: Bruno just uses more debt
Exactly. Both stands make €200 on €1,000: 20 %.
Ana, because she owes nothing
She takes less risk, yes. But the business is just as good.
**ROE** = profit ÷ the owners' money. Debt inflates it.
**ROIC** measures all the capital, debt included. It's much harder to inflate.
Does it create value or destroy it?
Money has a cost: the **cost of capital**, about 8-10 % a year. Here it's **9 %**. Which companies create value when they reinvest?
Creates value
Destroys value
ROIC of 25 % for years
Every euro reinvested earns almost three times what it costs.
ROIC of 6 %
It earns less than the 9 % that money costs.
Panadería Global: ROIC of 14.6 %
It beats the cost of capital comfortably.
ROE of 40 % thanks to lots of debt, with ROIC of 5 %
The ROE shines because of the debt; the business earns little.
Grows very fast with ROIC of 4 %
Growing like that destroys value: the more it grows, the worse.
ROIC of 18 % with no debt
It earns a lot on all its capital without relying on debt.
Sort the six companies.
A business **creates value** only if its **ROIC beats the cost of capital**. If it doesn't, the more it grows, the more value it destroys.
Compare each ROIC with 9 %. ROE isn't enough.
Does it earn more than money costs?
The compounding machines
Picture a company that reinvests **all** its profit at its ROIC. Its capital is **€1,000**. Watch how much it grows.
With an ROIC of 20 % reinvested for 10 years, how many times over does its capital multiply?
3 times: 20 % for 10 years
Just over 6 times
20 times
20 % on capital that keeps growing: 1.20 multiplied by itself 10 times gives **6.2**.
Over 10 years, find the ROIC that multiplies the capital 6 times or more.
The best businesses **reinvest at high ROIC** for years: at 20 %, capital multiplies 6.2 times in 10 years. It's an example, not a promise.
More than 6 times! That's compounding.
With an ROIC like that, it barely beats the cost of capital.
Turn up the ROIC and watch the curve

steps.title: Panadería Global's ROE and ROIC
steps.body:
• **ROE = net profit ÷ shareholders' equity.** 97.5 ÷ 450 = **21.7 %**. Sustained above **15 %**, it's very good.
• **ROIC = EBIT × (1 − tax) ÷ (equity + net debt).** 150 × 0.75 ÷ (450 + 320) = **14.6 %**. It has to beat the **cost of capital** (≈ 8-10 %).
steps.key: Look for businesses that turn every euro invested into much more than a euro, year after year.
steps.tip: Try it: ask Lumi what ROIC an excellent business has.

texts: A 12 % dividend
Marta
Look! This share pays a 12 % dividend. No savings account pays that.
Mind you, it's fallen 50 % this year.
What do you think is going on?
It's a bargain: collect the 12 % and wait
The yield has gone up because the price has collapsed, not because they're paying more.
The market expects the dividend to be cut
That's usually what it means. If the price halves, the yield doubles.
First check whether it earns what it pays out
Good question. And the collapsed price is already a clue.
**Dividend yield** = dividend ÷ price. Panadería Global: 0.50 ÷ 15 = **3.3 %**.
**Payout ratio** = dividend ÷ earnings. Panadería Global: 0.50 ÷ 0.975 = **51 %**.
Where does the dividend come from?
A high dividend is no use if it's cut tomorrow. **Sustainable** or **at risk**?
Sustainable
At risk
Pays out half of what it earns
Payout ratio of 50 %: it pays out and still reinvests the other half.
Payout ratio of 110 % three years running
It pays out more than it earns: it's dipping into cash or debt.
Pays the dividend with new debt
A sustainable dividend comes out of cash, not out of debt.
Its free cash flow covers the dividend twice over
It has cash to spare for paying out and investing.
Yields 12 % because the share has collapsed
Often, the market is expecting a cut.
Payout ratio of 40 % and rising profits
It has plenty of room to keep it, or raise it.
The dividend exceeds its free cash flow
If the cash doesn't stretch, the difference comes from debt.
Sort the seven dividends.
Before looking at how much it pays, look at **where it comes from**. A payout ratio above 80-90 % or a dividend bigger than free cash flow signals a **cut**.
Does it pay it out of earnings or with debt?
Sort each dividend

steps.title: A dividend isn't a gift
steps.body: When a company pays €1 per share, the share usually falls by around €1 that day: the money moves from the company to your pocket, and Hacienda (the Spanish tax authority) takes its cut. What counts is the **total return**.
steps.key: A sustainable dividend comes out of cash, not out of debt.
steps.tip: Try it: ask Lumi what payout puts a dividend at risk.

texts: Bringing the future to today
Your grandmother offers you **€100** today or in a few years' time: you'd rather have it today, right? Move the years and the **rate** you demand and see what that future payment is worth today.
What €100 in the future is worth today
At a 9 % rate, how much is €100 you'll get in a year's time worth today?
About €109
About €92
Exactly €100
100 ÷ 1.09 = **€91.74**: invest €91.74 today at 9 % and you'd have €100 in a year.
With the rate at 9 %, find how many years away that €100 is worth less than half today.
**Value today = future cash flow ÷ (1 + rate)^years.** At 9 %, €100 in 9 years' time is worth only €46 today: the further away and the higher the rate, **the less the future is worth**.
Less than half! Time weighs a lot.
If you demand a higher return, the future is worth less today.
Move the years and see what it's worth today
Leo's DCF
Leo
I've done Panadería Global's DCF! It's worth €19.6 and trades at €15.
Leo assumes: free cash flow of €1 per share, growing 6 % a year for 10 years and then 2 % forever. Rate: 9 %.
A 23 % margin. Shall I buy now?
What do you tell him?
Buy! The numbers don't lie
The numbers depend on the assumptions. Tweak them a little and you'll see.
Try slightly more cautious assumptions
Good thinking. Let's tweak the rate and the growth.
Buy a little and keep looking
Cautious. But first see how much the value changes.
A 10 % rate: about **€17**. 4 % growth: about **€16.9**.
Both at once: **€14.7**. Already below the price.
A DCF is for **thinking**, not for producing an exact figure.
Does the value go up or down?
A DCF is a machine made of assumptions. If you change one piece, does the estimated value go **up** or **down**?
Value goes up
Value goes down
You raise the discount rate from 9 % to 10 %
If you demand more, future money is worth less today.
You lower the expected growth
Less future cash, less value today.
The cash flows arrive sooner
The sooner you get paid, the less you discount.
Market interest rates rise
With higher interest rates, investors demand a higher rate.
You raise perpetual growth from 2 % to 3 %
The terminal value divides by (rate − growth): it goes up.
You lower the rate from 9 % to 8 %
The future counts for more today.
Place the six changes.
Higher rate or lower growth = **lower value**. Because each assumption moves the result a lot, a DCF gives you a **range**, not an exact number.
Think: is future money worth more or less today?
Does the value go up or down?

steps.title: The pieces of a DCF
steps.body:
1. Estimate **free cash flow** for the coming years.
2. Discount each cash flow back to today.
3. Add the **terminal value** (Gordon formula): next year's free cash flow ÷ (rate − perpetual growth).
4. Compare it with the price.

Panadería Global: 10 years of cash flows ≈ **€8.6** + terminal value (€26.1, brought back to today) ≈ **€11.0** = **€19.6**.
steps.key: If tweaking the assumptions slightly makes the value collapse, tread carefully.
steps.tip: Try it: ask Lumi what happens to the price if a company grows less than expected.

texts: Live through the dot-com bubble
Late 1998. Tech stocks are all the rage and the market keeps getting pricier. You invest **€10,000** in the Nasdaq 100, with real data. You can sell whenever you like.
Make it to the end, whether you sell or not.

With the S&P 500's CAPE at its record (44, December 1999), the Nasdaq 100 still rose until March 2000. Then it fell **83 %** and didn't regain its peak until 2015: **an extreme valuation doesn't tell you when**, but the risk was huge.
You've sold. Watch what happens next…
Your €10,000 is worth less than half. Will you hold on?
More than doubled! Valuations are already at record levels…
Hit «Start». You can sell whenever you like
«The market is really expensive»
Irene
October 2026.
I've read that the S&P 500's CAPE is at 41. What's that?
The price divided by average earnings over **10 years**, adjusted for inflation.
Average since 1871: about **17**. Record: **44**, in December 1999.
So it's about to crash! I'll sell everything and get back in when it drops.
What do you tell her?
Sell now, before it falls
The CAPE doesn't tell you **when**. It can stay expensive for years.
Adjust what you expect to earn and diversify across countries
That's it. A high CAPE points to **lower returns over 10 years**.
Do nothing: the CAPE is useless
It is useful: for expecting less, not for guessing next month.
Other regions trade at noticeably cheaper valuations. Another reason to diversify.

steps.title: What it tells you and what it doesn't
steps.body:
**Yes:** historically, a high CAPE has been linked to **lower returns over the following 10 years**.
**No:** it doesn't tell you **when** the market will fall; it can stay expensive for years.

Other regions trade at noticeably cheaper valuations: another argument for diversifying across countries.
steps.key: The CAPE is for adjusting your expectations, not for guessing next month.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, compare the S&P 500 with the IBEX 35 over 5 years.

u17l2-6.prompt: Why is EV/EBITDA useful for comparing companies with different levels of debt?
options: Because it adds net debt to the company's value
Because it only looks at the dividend
Because it ignores debt
u17l2-6.explanation: When you buy a whole company, you take on its debts too.

u17l2-7.prompt: Two companies with the same P/E can have very different EV/EBITDA ratios.
options: True
False
u17l2-7.explanation: If one has lots of debt, its EV is much larger than its market cap.

u17l2-8.prompt: A and B each have a market cap of €1,000m and EBITDA of €100m. A has no debt; B has €800m of net debt. A friend says they «cost the same». What do you tell them?
options: That B is cheaper because it has debt
That they're right: the market caps are the same
That B is more expensive: EV/EBITDA of 18 versus 10
u17l2-8.explanation: Enterprise value looks at the whole company, debt included.
feedback: Debt is something you owe, not a gift.
Market cap doesn't include debt: buy B and you also take on €800m that has to be paid back.

u17l2-10.prompt: According to the PEG, reasonable or expensive for its growth?
options: P/E 40, growing at 10 %
P/E 10, growing at 12 %
P/E 24, growing at 8 %
P/E 15, growing at 15 %
u17l2-10.explanation: PEG = P/E ÷ growth. 15 ÷ 15 = 1 and 10 ÷ 12 = 0.83: reasonable. 40 ÷ 10 = 4 and 24 ÷ 8 = 3: expensive for their growth.

u17l2-11.prompt: FitA and FitB, two made-up gym chains, trade at a P/E of 15. FitA has no debt; FitB has net debt equal to its stock market value. If you bought the whole company, which would be more expensive?
options: FitB: with its debt, its enterprise value is double
Both the same: they have the same P/E
FitA, because it doesn't make use of debt
u17l2-11.explanation: Enterprise value adds net debt to market cap. With the same P/E, the one that owes more is the more expensive to buy outright.
feedback: That's it: buying FitB, you also take on its debt. Its EV is twice its market cap.
The P/E doesn't see debt: that's why EV/EBITDA exists.
Owing nothing doesn't make the company dearer: quite the opposite, you have nothing to pay back.

u17l2-12.prompt: Three made-up companies. Which looks cheapest for how fast it grows?
options: P/E of 20 and growing at 5 % a year
P/E of 30 and growing at 30 % a year
P/E of 10 and growing at 2 % a year
u17l2-12.explanation: Compare the P/E with growth: 30 divided by 30 gives a PEG of 1; 20 by 5, 4; 10 by 2, 5. The lowest P/E is tempting, but it isn't cheap if the company barely grows.

u17l2-13.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: P/B is no use for banks
It may be cheap, but look at why the market distrusts its balance sheet
Yes, it's a sure bargain: buy as much as you can
u17l2-13.explanation: For banks and insurers P/B is very useful, but a very low one usually means the market doubts what its balance sheet is worth. Cheap isn't the same as safe.
feedback: Quite the opposite: for banks it's one of the most useful ratios.
OK: maybe its loans are worth less than it says.
If the market doubts its loans, that book value can shrink.
lines: This bank trades at half its book value.

u17l3-5.prompt: A very high ROE can be the result of the company having lots of debt.
options: True
False
u17l3-5.explanation: With little equity, any profit looks like a huge return.

u17l3-6.prompt: Why is ROIC more reliable than ROE for judging the business?
options: Because the tax authority calculates it
Because it includes debt in the capital
Because it always comes out higher
u17l3-6.explanation: ROE shoots up if the company takes on debt; ROIC, not so much.

u17l3-8.prompt: Cost of capital: 9 %. Rank these from best to worst business by ROIC.
options: ROIC of 15 %
ROIC of 9 %
ROIC of 4 %
ROIC of 30 %
u17l3-8.explanation: Above 9 % it creates value; at 9 %, it neither creates nor destroys it; below that, it destroys it.

u17l3-9.prompt: Laura is comparing two companies. A: ROE of 25 % with net debt/EBITDA of 5. B: ROE of 18 %, no debt and an ROIC of 18 %. Which looks like the better business?
options: A: its ROE is higher
B: it earns a lot on all its capital without relying on debt
There's no way to tell
u17l3-9.explanation: Look at ROE alongside ROIC and debt.
feedback: With that much debt, the ROE may come from leverage more than from the business.
Exactly: an 18 % ROIC with no debt is a quality business.
With ROE, ROIC and debt you can already get a pretty good idea.

u17l3-11.prompt: Two made-up cafés earn €100,000 a year each. The first needed €200,000 to open; the second, 2 million. Which is the better business?
options: The second: it's bigger
Both the same: they earn the same
The first: it earns the same with much less capital
u17l3-11.explanation: ROIC compares what a business earns with the capital it needs. With the same profit, the one that needs less capital is the better business and can grow without asking for as much money.
feedback: Bigger isn't better: it needs ten times more money to earn the same.
They earn the same, but one needs ten times more capital.
That's it: it returns 50 % on its capital; the second, only 5 %.

u17l3-12.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: ROE is useless
Yes: buy now
Check its debt and its ROIC first: debt inflates ROE
u17l3-12.explanation: A very high ROE can come from a great business or from lots of debt. ROIC, which counts all the capital, tells you which it is.
feedback: It's useful, but you have to look at it alongside debt and ROIC.
An ROE like that may come from debt more than from the business.
You're right: with little equity, any profit looks huge.
lines: This company has an ROE of 60 %.
It's the best business in the world!

u17l3-13.prompt: Which signs point to a quality business? Tick all that apply.
options: High ROE with hardly any debt
High ROE only thanks to lots of debt
Growing fast with an ROIC of 4 %
ROIC above the cost of capital for years
u17l3-13.explanation: Quality means earning a lot on all the capital without depending on debt. Growing with an ROIC below the cost of capital destroys value, however fast it is.

u17l4-4.prompt: Tick the messages that are signs of a scam or deception involving dividends.
options: The AGM approves a dividend of €0.50 per share, to be paid on 2 July.
I'll pay you a 3 % monthly «dividend» if you transfer your money to this account.
Live off dividends with €1,000: my course shows you how for €499.
🔥 Share with a 25 % ANNUAL dividend, GUARANTEED. Today only, limited places.
You've received €12.40 in dividends, net of withholding tax.
u17l4-4.explanation: Guaranteed returns, monthly «dividends» outside any regulated market and promises that you can live off your investments with €1,000 are classic signs of deception. At 4 %, €1,000 gives you about €40 a year.

u17l4-7.prompt: Bruno is comparing two shares by their dividend. A: 3.5 % yield, 50 % payout ratio and free cash flow that covers the dividend twice over. B: 9 % yield, 130 % payout ratio and rising debt. Which makes more sense?
options: It doesn't matter: dividends are guaranteed
Go for B: it pays almost three times as much
Go for A: its dividend is covered by earnings and cash
u17l4-7.explanation: Before looking at how much it pays, look at where the money comes from.
feedback: No share dividend is guaranteed.
It pays out more than it earns and borrows to do it: that 9 % could vanish overnight.
Exactly: a smaller but sustainable dividend is usually worth more than a high one that's at risk.

options: price
debt
sales
EPS
u17l4-10.explanation: How much of the earnings is paid out.

u17l4-11.prompt: You receive a dividend of €1 per share and that same day the share goes from €20 to €19, with no other news. Have you made money?
options: I've lost €1 per share
Yes: €1 free per share
Not from the dividend itself: that euro has moved from the share to your pocket
u17l4-11.explanation: A dividend isn't a gift: it comes out of the company's value. What matters is total return, price plus dividends.
feedback: Not that either: the share is worth €1 less, but you have that euro.
It isn't free: it comes out of the company's value, which falls by the same amount.
That's it: what counts is total return, and on top of that the taxman takes his share.

u17l4-13.prompt: Order these dividends from safest to most at risk.
options: Payout of 70 % and stable profits
Payout of 130 % paid with debt
Payout of 100 %: it pays out everything it earns
Payout of 40 % and growing profits
u17l4-13.explanation: The closer to or above 100 % the payout is, the less room is left if profit falls. Paying it with debt is the worst sign.

u17l5-6.prompt: What is a DCF mainly for?
options: Getting the exact value of a company
Knowing when the share price will go up
Thinking about what growth the price is assuming
u17l5-6.explanation: Small changes in the assumptions change the result a lot.

u17l5-8.prompt: Pablo does a DCF: a company trading at €60 is «worth» €120. To get there he assumed 25 % annual growth for 10 years and a 6 % rate. What should he do?
options: Go all in: it's worth double
Try more cautious assumptions and see how much the value changes
Post it on a forum
u17l5-8.explanation: A DCF is only as good as its assumptions.
feedback: His result depends on very optimistic assumptions: with more cautious ones, the «double» could disappear.
Good: if the value collapses with reasonable growth and a reasonable rate, the margin was an illusion.
Before convincing anyone else, convince yourself with cautious assumptions.

u17l5-10.prompt: Put the steps of a simplified DCF in order.
options: Discount each cash flow back to today at your rate
Calculate the terminal value and discount it
Add it all up and compare it with the price
Estimate free cash flow for the coming years
u17l5-10.explanation: Future, discounting, terminal value and comparison.

u17l5-11.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: Better to think in terms of a range and demand a good margin of safety
DCFs are useless
Perfect! If it trades at €47.31, it's cheap
u17l5-11.explanation: A DCF gives you a rough range, not an exact figure.
feedback: You're right: I move the rate by one point and get €40. Phew!
They're useful, for thinking. Not for giving you decimals.
One cent isn't a margin: your figure could be several euros out either way.
lines: My DCF says this share is worth exactly €47.32 🤓

u17l5-12.prompt: With a 9 % rate, which payment is worth more today?
options: €100 in 1 year
€100 in 10 years
€100 in 30 years
u17l5-12.explanation: The sooner the money arrives, the less you need to discount it. At 30 years, €100 is worth very little today at a 9 % rate: that's why the distant future weighs so little in a DCF.

u17l5-13.prompt: Iván and Sara value the same company with a 9 % rate. Iván assumes it will grow 30 % a year for 20 years; Sara, 7 % for 10 years and then 2 %. Which value is more useful for deciding?
options: Iván's: it comes out higher
Sara's: her assumptions are prudent and believable
Both the same: they use the same rate
u17l5-13.explanation: A DCF is only as good as its assumptions. With prudent assumptions, the value it gives helps you decide; with dream assumptions, it only gets your hopes up.
feedback: Higher isn't truer: it depends on almost impossible growth.
That's it: very few companies grow 30 % a year for 20 years.
The rate is the same, but growth changes everything.

u17l6-1.prompt: Look at the Nasdaq 100 from late 1997 to March 2000. What trend do you see? (Nasdaq 100 · weekly closes · up to the week of 06/03/2000)
options: Uptrend
Downtrend
Sideways
u17l6-1.explanation: A huge rise: valuations reached levels never seen before.

u17l6-3.prompt: December 1989: the Japanese stock market is trading at record valuations after a decade of euphoria. What did the Nikkei 225 do in the following years?
options: Up
Down
u17l6-3.explanation: As with the US CAPE, a very high valuation doesn't set a date: it only shifts the odds of what comes next.

u17l6-4.prompt: The CAPE divides the price by the average real earnings of the last ____ years.
u17l6-4.explanation: Ten years smooth out the economic cycle.

u17l6-5.prompt: What has the historical average of the S&P 500 CAPE been since 1871?
options: About 17
About 5
About 41
u17l6-5.explanation: In October 2026 it was around 41, well above that average.

u17l6-12.prompt: Two made-up stock markets: A trades at a CAPE of 40 and B at one of 15. You're investing for the next 10 years. What's most reasonable to expect?
options: That A will definitely fall this year
That A returns less than B, though I don't know when or by how much
That A returns more: if it's expensive, it's because it's doing well
u17l6-12.explanation: Historically, a high CAPE has gone with lower returns over 10 years. It helps you adjust what you expect and diversify, not guess the timing.
feedback: The CAPE doesn't say when: A can stay expensive for years.
That's it: paying a high price leaves less room, but the CAPE gives no dates.
Paying a high price leaves less room to make money later.

u17l6-13.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: Yes, get out now
Buy more with a loan
The CAPE doesn't say when: better adjust what you expect and diversify
u17l6-13.explanation: Getting out and back in means getting it right twice. A high CAPE calls for more modest expectations and diversifying across countries, not betting on a date.
feedback: It can stay expensive for years: the Nasdaq kept rising until March 2000.
Debt in an expensive market: risk on top of risk.
You're right: I'd have to get it right twice, getting out and getting back in.
lines: They say the market is really expensive.
I'll sell everything and get back in when it falls, right?
